title: Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning - CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning - Source Selection & Contract Types
subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Which condition strictly dictates the use of an Invitation for Bids (IFB) rather than a Request for Proposals (RFP)?
options: The agency knows what it needs but wants vendors to propose creative solutions.
Price is the primary or sole evaluation factor and the specifications are clear, definitive, and not subject to negotiation.
The procurement is for highly complex professional consulting services.
The agency wants to negotiate terms, scope, and price after bids are opened.
questions.explain: An IFB is used when requirements are precisely defined, no negotiation is required, and award is made to the lowest responsive and responsible bidder based exclusively on price.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A Request for Proposals (RFP) allows the public buyer to evaluate vendors based on:
options: Price alone.
A combination of price and scored non-price factors, such as technical approach, experience, and capability.
Geographic location only.
Qualifications exclusively, explicitly ignoring price.
questions.explain: The RFP method is utilized when price is not the sole determining factor. It allows for the weighted scoring of qualitative factors (experience, methodology) alongside pricing, seeking the 'best value'.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Under Qualifications-Based Selection (QBS) per the Brooks Act, how is price handled during the procurement of Architecture and Engineering (A&E) services?
options: Price is weighted at exactly 50% of the evaluation score.
Vendors submit sealed pricing, and the lowest price is awarded immediately.
Price is completely excluded from the initial evaluation; the agency selects the most qualified firm and then negotiates a fair and reasonable price.
Price is used as a tie-breaker if two firms are equally qualified.
questions.explain: QBS requires that A&E firms be evaluated purely on their technical competence and experience. Price cannot be requested or considered until the most qualified firm is identified, at which point negotiations begin.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: In a 'Multi-Step Bidding' process, what occurs during Step One?
options: Unpriced technical proposals are evaluated to determine which vendors offer acceptable, qualifying solutions.
Sealed prices are opened, and the lowest bidder wins.
The agency issues an immediate payment to the short-listed vendors.
Best and Final Offers (BAFO) are requested.
questions.explain: Multi-step bidding (often two-step IFB) begins with an evaluation of unpriced technical proposals. Only firms whose technical proposals are deemed acceptable move on to Step Two, where their sealed price bids are opened.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Which contract type places the maximum financial risk on the supplier and the minimum financial risk on the buyer?
options: Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF).
Time and Materials (T&M).
Firm-Fixed Price (FFP).
Cost-Plus-Percentage-of-Cost (CPPC).
questions.explain: In a Firm-Fixed Price (FFP) contract, the vendor agrees to deliver the goods/services for a specified price. If their costs run higher than expected, the vendor absorbs the loss, placing risk squarely on the supplier.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A Time and Materials (T&M) contract should primarily be used when:
options: The exact scope and duration of the work are definitively known before contract execution.
It is impossible at the time of award to accurately estimate the extent or duration of the work, or to anticipate future costs.
Purchasing commercial-off-the-shelf commodities.
The buyer wants to eliminate the need to monitor contractor hours.
questions.explain: T&M contracts are used only when uncertainties involved in contract performance make it impossible to state a fixed cost upfront. They require high buyer oversight to ensure efficiency.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: To mitigate the extreme risk to the buyer in a Time and Materials (T&M) contract, the buyer must include a:
options: Guaranteed minimum profit clause.
Not-to-Exceed (NTE) financial cap.
Clause that guarantees indefinite employment to the contractor's staff.
Cost-Plus-Percentage-of-Cost addendum.
questions.explain: Because T&M contracts pay per hour and per material unit, costs can spiral. A Not-To-Exceed (NTE) cap limits the buyer's maximum financial exposure, requiring the contractor to stop work or seek a modification before exceeding the cap.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Why is the Cost-Plus-Percentage-of-Cost (CPPC) contract universally prohibited in public procurement?
options: Because it transfers too much risk to the vendor.
Because it is mathematically impossible to calculate.
Because it incentivizes the contractor to intentionally inflate their costs to increase their total profit.
Because it is only allowed for federal agencies, not local ones.
questions.explain: In a CPPC contract, the vendor's profit increases directly as their costs increase. This creates a perverse incentive for the vendor to be inefficient and inflate costs, harming the public taxpayer.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: An agency needs a continuous supply of janitorial paper products throughout the year but doesn't have storage space. They issue a solicitation for an estimated quantity, guaranteeing delivery when requested. What contract type is best?
options: A Time and Materials contract.
A Firm-Fixed Price spot purchase.
An Indefinite Delivery/Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) or Requirements term contract.
A Cost-Sharing contract.
questions.explain: IDIQ (or term/requirements) contracts establish pricing for a defined period based on estimated quantities. Deliveries are made 'as needed' via task or purchase orders, solving storage constraints while locking in price.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: What is the defining feature of a 'Requirements Contract' compared to a standard IDIQ?
options: It legally obligates the agency to purchase all its actual requirements for those specific items exclusively from the awarded vendor.
It requires the agency to purchase exactly 10,000 units.
It allows the agency to purchase the items from any vendor on the street.
It requires the vendor to hire subcontractors.
questions.explain: A requirements contract promises the vendor exclusivity: all of the agency's actual needs for that commodity during the contract term MUST be purchased from that vendor, even if the actual quantity ends up being zero.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A Blanket Purchase Agreement (BPA) is best described as:
options: A legally binding contract that guarantees a vendor $100,000 in sales.
A simplified method of filling anticipated repetitive needs for supplies or services by establishing 'charge accounts' with qualified sources.
A procurement method used exclusively for emergency construction.
A multi-million dollar IT implementation contract.
questions.explain: A BPA is not a contract; it is an arrangement—similar to setting up a corporate charge account—that allows authorized individuals to make repetitive, small-dollar purchases quickly without issuing multiple POs.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Which of the following scenarios best justifies a Sole Source procurement?
options: The end-user really likes the sales representative from Company A.
Company B is located directly across the street from the agency headquarters.
The required part is patented, protected by copyright, and is only available directly from the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) with no authorized distributors.
The buyer forgot to start the RFP process on time and needs the goods next week.
questions.explain: Sole source is justified when there is only one viable source in the marketplace capable of fulfilling the requirement, such as for patented proprietary parts or OEM-exclusive maintenance.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: An agency needs to clear debris after a devastating hurricane hits the city. Which procurement method is most appropriate given the circumstances?
options: Sole Source procurement.
Emergency procurement.
A formal six-month RFP process.
Multi-step IFB.
questions.explain: Emergency procurements are utilized when there is an immediate threat to public health, welfare, or safety. They bypass standard formal solicitation timeframes to deploy immediate, necessary resources.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A parks department wishes to hire a company to run food kiosks. The company will retain a portion of the sales and pay the rest to the city. What type of contract is this?
options: A Cost-Reimbursement contract.
A Revenue-Generating (or Concession) contract.
A Time and Materials contract.
A Grant Agreement.
questions.explain: Revenue-generating or concession contracts authorize a private vendor to provide a service to the public on government property. Instead of the government paying the vendor, the vendor pays the government a percentage of the revenue generated.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Job Order Contracting (JOC) is a method primarily used for:
options: Hiring temporary administrative staffing.
Procuring extremely large, complex, ground-up architectural design projects.
Performing repetitive, small-to-medium construction, repair, and renovation projects based on a preset catalog of pricing (Unit Price Book).
Buying commercial off-the-shelf software.
questions.explain: JOC is an indefinite delivery contract used for minor construction and renovation. Contractors bid a multiplier (coefficient) against a pre-priced catalog of construction tasks (a Unit Price Book).
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A buyer is using a Reverse Auction platform to purchase bulk rock salt. In a reverse auction:
options: Vendors bid increasingly higher prices until the agency agrees to buy.
Vendors submit downward-competing, real-time prices during a defined time window until the lowest price is achieved.
The buyer auctions off agency surplus property to the highest bidder.
Technical proposals are negotiated before sealed bids are opened.
questions.explain: Unlike a traditional auction where prices go up, a reverse auction involves vendors competing to sell their goods to the buyer by continuously bidding lower prices in a transparent, real-time digital environment.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: During an RFP evaluation, the committee decides they need final pricing concessions from the top three shortlisted firms after discussions. The buyer will request a:
options: Best and Final Offer (BAFO).
Notice of Intent to Award.
Sole Source Exemption.
Change Order.
questions.explain: A BAFO is a formal request for pricing and/or technical adjustments from shortlisted vendors in an RFP process, typically requested after negotiations or discussions have concluded.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A multi-year contract for fuel includes an Economic Price Adjustment (EPA) clause. The purpose of this clause is to:
options: Ensure the vendor makes exactly 10% profit regardless of cost.
Allow for upward or downward adjustment of the contract price based on an agreed-upon, independent market index (e.g., OPIS or CPI).
Penalize the vendor for late deliveries.
Allow the buyer to cancel the contract if budgets are cut.
questions.explain: EPA clauses shift some of the market volatility risk (like fluctuating fuel prices) from the vendor to the buyer by allowing the price to move up or down in correlation with an independent economic index.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Before issuing a highly sensitive solicitation for a security system, the buyer issues a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) to establish a shortlist of vendors who meet stringent security clearances. This is known as:
options: Post-qualification.
Pre-qualification.
Value analysis.
Piggybacking.
questions.explain: Pre-qualification is the process of vetting vendor capabilities, financial stability, and security clearances before allowing them to submit a technical proposal or bid in the actual solicitation.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: In evaluating an IFB, a bidder forgets to sign their bid document. This is generally considered a matter of being:
options: Non-responsible.
Non-responsive.
In breach of contract.
Guilty of collusion.
questions.explain: Responsiveness relates to whether the bid fully complied with all the material requirements of the solicitation document itself (e.g., signatures, bid bonds). Responsibility relates to the vendor's capability to perform (financials, experience).
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: In an RFP for consulting services, the evaluation criteria must be drafted. Best practice dictates that the criteria weightings (e.g., 40% Price, 60% Technical) should be:
options: Determined after reading the proposals to ensure the preferred vendor wins.
Established prior to the issuance of the RFP and clearly stated in the solicitation document.
Kept secret from the vendors.
Decided solely by the procurement officer without end-user input.
questions.explain: Evaluation criteria and their relative weights must be determined during pre-solicitation planning and clearly published in the RFP to ensure fairness, transparency, and objective scoring.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: To align vendor behavior with agency goals, a buyer designs a contract that awards bonus payments if a construction project finishes 30 days early. This is a(n):
options: Incentive contract.
Time and Materials contract.
Liquidated damages clause.
Cost-Plus-Percentage-of-Cost contract.
questions.explain: Incentive contracts are designed to motivate the contractor to achieve specific performance goals, such as early completion or cost savings, by offering a financial bonus.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A 'Single Source' procurement differs from a 'Sole Source' procurement in that:
options: There is no difference; the terms mean exactly the same thing.
In a single source, multiple suppliers exist, but the agency strategically chooses to contract with only one specific vendor.
Single source procurements require federal approval.
Sole source procurements apply only to commodities, while single source applies to services.
questions.explain: Sole source means only one vendor exists in the marketplace. Single source means competition exists, but the agency makes a deliberate, strategic, and justified choice to source from only one vendor (e.g., standardization).
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Which of the following describes a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF) contract?
options: The vendor is reimbursed for actual allowable costs, plus a predetermined, fixed sum of profit that does not change with actual cost variances.
The vendor receives a percentage of whatever their final costs are.
The agency pays a single flat rate for the entire project upfront.
The vendor agrees to perform the work for free but retains the patent rights.
questions.explain: In a CPFF contract, the buyer reimburses actual allowable costs, but the fee (profit) is a fixed dollar amount negotiated upfront. Unlike CPPC, the profit doesn't increase if costs overrun, mitigating some risk.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: When assessing vendor responsibility prior to an award, a public procurement professional might evaluate:
options: Whether the vendor signed the bid form properly.
The financial health, equipment capacity, and past performance references of the vendor.
Whether the vendor submitted the bid before the deadline.
The number of typos in the vendor's cover letter.
questions.explain: Responsibility refers to the bidder's capability to fully perform the contract requirements. It is determined by analyzing their financial resources, experience, equipment, and past performance record.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning
